DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
This review finds that the study's three main conclusions don't follow from its own data:

1. **Participation did not "hold up across houses and flats."** Table 1 shows 66% in houses against 21% in flats, more than a threefold gap. The case for one uniform service rests on the opposite reading.
2. **The tonnage projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the pilot data.** The pilot's overall rate was 57%, but Section 3 applies 64%. Corrected, the tonnage falls by roughly 11–13%, and so does the disposal saving.
3. **Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage.** Its contracted capacity is 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029, against a forecast of about 2,900–3,300. Roughly 40% of the food waste has nowhere local to go, and the cost of sending it 46 miles isn't included.

Fixing just the participation rate pushes the net cost slightly *above* the £520,000 allocation, before the capacity gap is addressed. "Fully funded" doesn't hold as written.

The cost table arithmetic is correct, and the pilot itself is a genuinely useful piece of evidence. The problems are in how it's interpreted and what the projection leaves out.

## 1. The flats finding is reversed

| | Participation | Food waste per participating household |
|---|---|---|
| Houses | 66% | 1.9 kg/week |
| Flats | **21%** | 1.4 kg/week |

Section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types" and concludes no separate approach for flats is needed. The table shows the reverse. Low participation in flats is a well-known pattern in food waste schemes, usually because of storage space, communal bin areas and the distance to the collection point. With about 10,400 flats in the district (20% of 52,000), this matters.

The honest reading of the pilot is that the service works well for houses and poorly for flats as designed. The roll-out plan should include a flats-specific approach, such as communal food waste bins, different caddy arrangements or targeted engagement, along with its cost. This is the finding that most needs correcting, because the recommendation of a uniform service depends on it.

## 2. The projection uses 64% instead of 57%

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." No 64% appears in Table 1; the overall figure is **57%**. Since the pilot's housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's, 57% is the directly applicable figure.

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| Study as written (64% × 1.9 kg) | **~3,290 t** |
| Pilot overall (57% × 1.9 kg) | ~2,930 t |
| By housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg; flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | **~2,870 t** |

The housing-type calculation:
- Houses: 41,600 × 66% × 1.9 kg × 52 ≈ 2,713 t.
- Flats: 10,400 × 21% × 1.4 kg × 52 ≈ 159 t.

The "All" row's 1.9 kg is also rounded up. The weighted average is about 1.86 kg.

The disposal saving falls accordingly: 2,870 t × £74 ≈ **£212,000**, not £243,000.

**Further caveat:** the pilot ran January to June, in its first six months. Participation in new food waste schemes often dips after the novelty wears off, and summer (flies, smell) can affect it. It's worth stating that the projection may be optimistic for that reason.

## 3. Brookfield can only take 1,800 tonnes

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer "up to 1,800 tonnes a year" until its expansion in 2029. At either tonnage estimate, that leaves a large shortfall:

| | Study tonnage | Corrected tonnage |
|---|---|---|
| Projected | 3,290 t | ~2,870 t |
| Brookfield capacity | 1,800 t | 1,800 t |
| **Shortfall** | **~1,490 t** | **~1,070 t** |

The only alternative named is an AD plant **46 miles away**. The study includes no gate fee for it, no haulage or transfer costs, and no extra vehicle or crew time if collection vehicles have to travel there themselves. Those costs will reduce the £74/t saving on the shortfall tonnage, and could wipe it out. Separately collected food waste presumably can't simply go back into incineration, so this needs a costed solution.

**This also undermines the timeline.** If the 2029 expansion slips, the shortfall continues. The cover note's "Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is true for only about 60% of the waste.

## 4. "Fully funded" doesn't survive the corrections

| | Study | Corrected tonnage only |
|---|---|---|
| Gross cost | £733,400 | £733,400 |
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | ~£212,000 |
| **Net cost** | **£490,400** | **~£521,000** |
| Provisional allocation | £520,000 | £520,000 |
| **Headroom** | **+£29,600** | **~–£1,000** |

The corrected figure is just over the allocation, and that's *before*:
- the cost of handling about 1,070 tonnes beyond Brookfield's capacity,
- any flats-specific provision,
- the cost omissions listed below.

The allocation is also **provisional**. Even on the study's own figures, the headroom was only about 6%. The paper should describe the service as "substantially but not fully funded on current estimates," and show the gap.

## 5. Costs missing from Table 2

The Table 2 arithmetic is correct:
- Vehicles: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400.
- Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000.
- Total: £733,400.

But several items appear to be missing:
- **Cover for crews.** Six crews with no spare drivers or loaders won't cover holiday and sickness. Agency or relief staff usually add 10–15%.
- **Supervision and management**, and depot space or parking for six extra vehicles.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** from Section 6.
- **Capital financing.** Depreciation spreads the £990,000 vehicle cost, but the money is spent up front. The financing or borrowing cost isn't shown.
- **Ongoing liners.** Section 6 mentions a three-month supply. Confirm whether the £88,000 assumes the Council provides liners indefinitely.
- **The basis for six vehicles.** There's no round modelling shown, and the capacity issue may change it if some loads must travel 46 miles.
- **Inflation and pay awards** over the funding period.

## 6. The implementation timetable has no slack

- The study is dated October 2026. Cabinet approval and the vehicle order must both happen by December.
- Vehicles arrive in March 2027, and crews must be trained on them in the same month.
- About 52,000 caddy packs must be delivered in March.
- Collections start on 5 April.

A late vehicle delivery or a caddy supplier problem leaves no buffer. The paper should name a contingency, such as hired vehicles, a phased start by area, or a fallback start date.

## 7. Smaller points

- **81% satisfaction** is of *surveyed* pilot households. Give the response rate, and note that respondents are likely to over-represent participants (43% of households didn't take part).
- **The contamination checks** under 2% are encouraging. Say how many spot checks there were.
- **The cover note says "every cost line is shown."** That overstates it, given the omissions above.

## What holds up

- The **pilot design** is sound: 4,000 households, mixed housing and settlement types, the same collection day as existing bins, and data broken down by housing type.
- The **participation and per-household figures in Table 1** are internally consistent (2,112 ÷ 3,200 = 66%; 168 ÷ 800 = 21%; 2,280 ÷ 4,000 = 57%).
- **Low contamination and good satisfaction among participants** are real positives.
- The **cost table arithmetic** and the **£74/t saving** per diverted tonne (£112 − £38) are correct.
- **Working back from the vehicle lead time** is the right way to build the timetable.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet

1. Rewrite the flats finding, and add a costed flats-specific approach.
2. Re-run the projection at 57%, or by housing type (about 2,870 t), with a sensitivity range for a post-novelty drop in participation.
3. Set out how the tonnage above 1,800 t will be treated until 2029, and what it will cost.
4. Restate the net cost against the provisional £520,000, and show the gap and how it would be funded.
5. Add the missing cost lines and show the basis for six vehicles.
6. Add timetable contingencies.

The roll-out is a legal requirement, so the question for Cabinet isn't really *whether* to proceed. It's what the service will cost and how the gap will be met. A corrected paper is far safer to take to Cabinet than one that later turns out to be under-funded by a margin the pilot data already showed.
